title: "Where Machines Fail"
---

::: {.quest-dialog}
**Prerequisites:** Tokens, Not Letters. **Objective:** sort jobs into "ask the model" and "run a script", and name the other ways a model fails with one mitigation each.
**Time:** about 15 minutes. <span class="ao-badge">Last verified (docs, not run): the sources listed in `research/failure-modes.md` (sections 6 and 7) on 2026-11-16. Verified: ran `echo banana | grep -o n | wc -l` and `grep -c '>'` on a three-record mock file. Items marked "general practice" or "Not checked:" are not from a source.</span>

A language model is good at some jobs and bad at others. The skill is knowing which is which before you trust the output. This quest does not say you must use a model for anything. It says where the risk sits if you do.

## Good jobs: the result is checkable

Models are generally useful where you can read the result, or run it, and judge it yourself (our inference from the research notes):

- summarising text
- drafting prose, such as a README or a methods first draft
- explaining code or an error message
- converting formats, for example a samplesheet CSV to JSON
- first drafts of code that you will then test

**Caveat for summaries.** A summary can leave things out or bend them. A peer-reviewed study of the older, pre-chat generation of summarisation models (Maynez et al., ACL 2020) found substantial unfaithful content in every system tested. That evidence is dated, but the direction still applies. We found no published faithfulness rate for current Claude on scientific papers. So spot-check against the source: numbers, gene and sample names, direction of effect, negations. Omissions are harder to see, so skim the abstract and limitations yourself. Asking the model to quote the supporting lines first also helps; the Anthropic docs recommend quote-first extraction.

## Bad job: exact counting and arithmetic

Ask a model: "How many n are in banana?" The right answer is 2 (b-a-n-a-n-a). A model can get this wrong, and can be wrong with full confidence. A leading explanation is the one from the last quest: it reads tokens, not letters (see Tokens, Not Letters). Be honest about the state of the science, though. Some papers propose tokenisation as the cause (arXiv 2505.14172, arXiv 2410.19730), and another study (CharBench, arXiv 2508.02591) finds it only weakly related to correctness, with word length and the true count mattering more. **The cause is debated. The fix is not.**

The fix is to run a script. Verified: ran this on macOS:

```bash
echo banana | grep -o n | wc -l
```

It printed `       2` (the macOS `wc` pads with spaces; the number is 2). One study (arXiv 2410.14166) reports that coding models asked to write Python for such counting tasks do them essentially perfectly. So a model that **writes the script** is fine. A model that "does the sum in its head" is not.

The bioinformatics versions of the same trap:

| You want | Give it to |
|---|---|
| Number of sequences in a FASTA | `grep -c '>' file.fa` (Verified: ran on a three-record mock file, printed 3), or `seqkit stats` |
| GC content, read length statistics | a script or `seqkit`, run by the agent, with the code visible |
| A p-value or any test statistic | a stats library in a script you can read and re-run |
| Sum or mean of a column | `awk`, or a script, never a number stated in prose |

Rule of thumb: never trust a count the agent states in prose. Ask for the command and its output.

::: {.panel-tabset group="companion"}

## Claude Code

It can run Bash and write scripts, so ask: "write and run a command for this, and show me both the command and its output."

## OpenCode + Ollama

Same rule. Not checked: how reliable small local models are at this. General practice: assume they are no better at counting, and insist on a script.

:::

## Other ways it fails

| Failure mode | What it looks like | What to do | Quest |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hallucination | A plausible DOI, gene ID or tool flag that does not exist | Allow "I don't know"; ask for word-for-word quotes first; restrict to supplied documents; look up every ID in PubMed or Ensembl, or run the tool's `--help` | Spot the Mirage |
| Sycophancy | Agrees with your wrong hypothesis, or softens a correct criticism when you push back (Sharma et al., arXiv 2310.13548) | General practice: ask for the strongest case against your idea, and do not reveal your preferred answer | none yet |
| Long-context degradation | Accuracy and recall drop as input grows ("context rot", per Anthropic's docs); relevant text in the middle is used less (arXiv 2307.03172) | Curate input: head, counts, filtered tables; start fresh for a new task | The Context Window |
| Instruction drift | An early instruction is forgotten, for example after compaction | Short instructions file; a hook for must-never rules (Claude Code) | The Context Window |
| Non-determinism | The same prompt can give different answers | Not checked in the official docs. General practice: run twice and compare; record command, model and version; treat the script it wrote as the reproducible part | Same Every Time |
| Overconfidence | Says it is done when it is not, often because it had no way to check | Give it a check to run (tests, row counts, md5) and read the output | none yet |
| Prompt injection | A README, PDF or FASTA header contains instructions the agent follows | Treat fetched content as data; review commands before approving; no system is fully immune | Plug In a Server |
| Stale knowledge | Newer tool versions or database releases postdate its training | Check `--version` and the current docs. Current Claude models list a June 2026 cutoff | none yet |

## The decision rule

**Can I check the result cheaply and independently?** If yes, ask the model: a bad answer will show. If the answer must be exactly right and cannot be checked, use a script.

<div data-ao-honour="count-letter" data-xp="20">Ask a model to count one letter in a long word (or a mock 40-letter DNA string), then check it with <code>grep -o</code> and <code>wc -l</code>. Note whether it was right, and how sure it sounded. One try proves nothing; it is a demonstration.</div>
<div data-ao-honour="spot-check-summary" data-xp="20">Have a model summarise a methods paragraph you wrote. Check every number, name and negation against your original, and note anything omitted.</div>
